summary: Hebrew says “my, your, his …” in two ways. (1) Everyday: the noun with the article, then שֶׁל “of” with a personal ending — הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי “my house”, literally “the house of-me”. The endings give שֶׁלִּי, שֶׁלְּךָ (to a man), שֶׁלָּךְ (to a woman), שֶׁלּוֹ, שֶׁלָּהּ, שֶׁלָּנוּ, שֶׁלָּכֶם, שֶׁלָּכֶן, שֶׁלָּהֶם, שֶׁלָּהֶן; they never agree with the thing owned — only the owner’s person, gender and number count (הָאָחוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ “his sister”). With a name or a noun as owner: הַתִּיק שֶׁל דָּנָה “Dana’s bag”. (2) The possessive suffix on the noun itself: אָחִי “my brother”, אִשְׁתִּי “my wife”, הוֹרַי “my parents”. For most nouns it is formal or written (אִמִּי, בְּנִי), but some family words take it in everyday speech too: אִשְׁתִּי, בַּעֲלִי, אָחִי, אֲחוֹתִי. A noun with a suffix is already definite and takes no הַ. The family words אִמָּא, אַבָּא, סַבָּא, סָבְתָא work like names: אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי, without הַ.

blocks.caption: The suffixes are the endings of שֶׁל and לְ; אָח and אָב add -ִי- (אָחִיו), feminines in -ָה show their old -ת- (אִשָּׁה → אִשְׁתִּי).

blocks.title: The noun must be definite
blocks.text: “My house” is הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי, with הַ. Without it, בַּיִת שֶׁלִּי means “a house of mine” (הוּא חָבֵר שֶׁלִּי “he’s a friend of mine”). אִמָּא, אַבָּא, סַבָּא and סָבְתָא are used like names: אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי.

blocks.title: It follows the owner, not the thing
blocks.text: שֶׁלּוֹ is “his”, שֶׁלָּהּ “her” — whatever the thing: הָאָחוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ “his sister”, הַבֵּן שֶׁלָּהּ “her son”. The word never changes for the thing owned: הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי, הַמִּטָּה שֶׁלִּי, הַסְּפָרִים שֶׁלִּי. To one person: שֶׁלְּךָ to a man, שֶׁלָּךְ to a woman. And the same שֶׁל serves for everything owned — a relative, a part of the body or a thing.

blocks.title: Which style?
blocks.text: Everyday: noun + שֶׁל (אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי, הַבֵּן שֶׁלִּי). Formal or written: the suffix (אִמִּי, בְּנִי). Some family words take the suffix in everyday speech too: אִשְׁתִּי, בַּעֲלִי, אָחִי, אֲחוֹתִי. A noun with a suffix is definite already: never *הָאָחִי.

items: formal and some family words: the suffix, no הַ

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Who is the owner (person, gender, number)?
Am I talking to a man or a woman?
Does my noun have הַ (or is it אִמָּא, אַבָּא …)?

askYourself: Who owns it — which person, gender and number? → שֶׁלִּי, שֶׁלּוֹ, שֶׁלָּהּ, שֶׁלָּנוּ …
Am I speaking to one man or one woman? → שֶׁלְּךָ / שֶׁלָּךְ; to a group → שֶׁלָּכֶם / שֶׁלָּכֶן.
Does the noun have הַ? It must — except אִמָּא, אַבָּא, סַבָּא, סָבְתָא and names.
Everyday or formal? → noun + שֶׁל (אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי), or the suffix (אִמִּי).
Is it a suffix form (אָחִי, אִשְׁתִּי)? → then no הַ and no שֶׁל.
steps: Choose שֶׁל + ending, or the suffix.
Give the noun הַ when you use שֶׁל.

traps: *בַּיִת שֶׁלִּי for “my house” — say הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי (without הַ it means “a house of mine”).
*הָאָחִי — a noun with a suffix never takes הַ: אָחִי.
שֶׁלִּי does not change for the thing owned: הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי, הַמִּטָּה שֶׁלִּי, הַסְּפָרִים שֶׁלִּי.
his / her follow the owner: הָאָחוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ “his sister”, הָאָח שֶׁלָּהּ “her brother”.
שֶׁלְּךָ is to a man, שֶׁלָּךְ to a woman.
*אִמָּאִי — “my mum” is אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי; the suffix form belongs to the formal אֵם: אִמִּי.

seeAlso.note: Arabic puts the owner as a suffix on the noun in everyday speech (بَيْتِي “my house”, أَخِي “my brother”) — the form Hebrew keeps for formal style and some family words.
German possessives stand before the noun and agree with it (mein Bruder, meine Schwester, meinen Bruder); Hebrew שֶׁלִּי follows the noun and never agrees with it.
Chinese uses 的 after the owner (我的书) and drops it with close family (我妈妈) — as Hebrew drops הַ in אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי.

notes.text: ο αδερφός μου — article + noun + “of me” — has the same order as הָאָח שֶׁלִּי, and as in Greek the possessive word does not agree with the thing owned. The suffix (אָחִי) has no Greek match.
Turkish kardeşim “my brother” is a suffix, like Hebrew אָחִי; but Hebrew uses the suffix mostly in formal style and says הָאָח שֶׁלִּי in everyday speech.
Russian мой / моя / моё agree with the thing owned; Hebrew שֶׁלִּי never does — it follows only the owner: הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי, הַמִּטָּה שֶׁלִּי.

Spanish mi / mis come before the noun and agree in number with it; Hebrew שֶׁלִּי comes after a definite noun and never changes for it: הַסְּפָרִים שֶׁלִּי. Unlike su, Hebrew separates “his” and “her”: שֶׁלּוֹ / שֶׁלָּהּ.
“His” and “her” follow the owner, as in English (הָאָחוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ “his sister”); but the noun needs the article: הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי, literally “the house of me”.
son / sa follow the thing owned (sa sœur is “his” or “her sister”); Hebrew follows the owner: הָאָחוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ “his sister”, הָאָחוֹת שֶׁלָּהּ “her sister”.
mein / meine come before the noun and agree with it; Hebrew שֶׁלִּי follows a definite noun and does not change for it.
Hindi मेरा / मेरी / मेरे agree with the thing owned and come first; Hebrew שֶׁלִּי comes after the noun and never agrees with it.
Persian puts the owner after the noun, with ezafe or a suffix (کتابِ من / کتابم); Hebrew has both ways too: הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי (everyday) and the suffix (formal).
Marathi माझा / माझी / माझे agree with the thing owned and come before it; Hebrew שֶׁלִּי follows the noun and depends only on the owner.
Arabic uses the suffix every day (أَخِي, كِتَابِي); Hebrew uses it mainly in formal style and with some family words, and otherwise says הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי — Standard Arabic has no word like שֶׁל.
Japanese puts the owner first with の (私の本); Hebrew puts it after the noun: הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי “the book of me”.
Korean puts the owner first (제 책); Hebrew puts it after: הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי.
Finnish also has possessive suffixes (kirjani “my book”, often with minun in front); Hebrew has suffixes too (אָחִי), but everyday speech prefers הָאָח שֶׁלִּי.
Hungarian marks the thing owned with a suffix (könyvem); Hebrew has such suffixes (אָחִי, אִשְׁתִּי), but everyday speech mostly uses שֶׁל + ending.
Swahili puts the possessive after the noun (kitabu changu), as Hebrew does (הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי); but Swahili -angu agrees with the noun’s class, while שֶׁלִּי never changes.
Luganda also puts the possessive after the noun (ekitabo kyange “my book”) and makes it agree with the noun’s class; Hebrew שֶׁלִּי stays the same for every noun.
Chinese puts the owner first with 的 (我的书); Hebrew puts it after — הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי — and the noun takes the article.
Vietnamese also puts the owner after the noun, often with của (sách của tôi); Hebrew שֶׁל is the same idea — הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי — with the article on the noun.
Inuktitut marks the owner with a suffix on the noun — “my house” is one word; Hebrew has such suffixes too (אָחִי), but everyday speech uses שֶׁל: הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי.
